papers.title: GSP: a multi-scale metric for evaluation of 3D RNA structure predictions
papers.summary: Abstract Motivation Accurate prediction of RNA 3D structures remains a central challenge in structural bioinformatics, necessitating reliable measures to quantify similarity between predicted models and experimentally determined reference structures. Currently, many scoring functions are available to assess different aspects of the tertiary structures of biomolecules. On the one hand, global measures average local irregularities, so that structures with distortions in different regions might generally be considered structurally similar. On the other hand, local conformational measures focus on specific inter-residue interactions and often fail to capture the broader topological context. Thus, there is a lack of methods capable of comprehensively assessing structural discrepancies across various spatial scales. Results To address this gap, we introduce Geometric Spherical Precision (GSP), a novel multi-scale score that assesses the quality of 3D RNA and RNP complex predictions. It integrates multiple partial scores computed from local geometric agreements into a single, easy-to-read, normalized score for ranking these predictions. We demonstrate that GSP reliably identifies models with comparable overall deviations, while maintaining strong agreement with global measures. These properties make it a useful tool for benchmarking and comparing 3D RNA structures and RNP complexes. Availability and Implementation The GSP script and evaluation results against state-of-the-art measures on the RNA-Puzzles and CASP15 datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19608328

papers.title: BioBatchNet: A Dual-Encoder Framework for Robust Batch Effect Correction in Imaging Mass Cytometry
papers.summary: Abstract Motivation Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC) is a cutting-edge technology for analysing spatially resolved protein expression at the single-cell level. However, its downstream analyses are often hindered by batch effects, which introduce systematic biases and obscure biological variations. Existing correction methods, largely developed for scRNA-seq data, face challenges in adapting to IMC data due to differences in data characteristics. Moreover, these methods struggle to achieve precise control, leading to either over-correction by removing critical biological information, or under-correction by leaving residual batch effects. Furthermore, IMC data often feature overlapping cell populations, complicating clustering and downstream analysis. These challenges underscore the need for a robust and controllable batch effect correction approach tailored to IMC data. Results We present BioBatchNet, a dual-encoder framework utilising adversarial training to explicitly disentangle batch-specific and biological signals. BioBatchNet enables controllable batch effect correction, balancing correction with preservation of biological variation. We evaluated BioBatchNet on three IMC datasets, where it outperformed seven benchmarking methods with robustness in both correction and biological signal conservation. Additionally, we developed a Constrained-Pairwise-Clustering (CPC) method, which employs constrained pairs to improve clustering performance, even in datasets with overlapping cell populations. To validate its generalisability, we adapted BioBatchNet for scRNA-seq datasets by altering the data likelihood from Gaussian to Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial distribution. This adapted version achieved competitive performance across four scRNA-seq datasets, obtaining the highest overall score on three of them. These results demonstrate BioBatchNet’s generalisability and robustness in correcting batch effects across diverse single-cell datasets and underscore its potential for large-scale biological analyses. all_papers.title: GSP: a multi-scale metric for evaluation of 3D RNA structure predictions
all_papers.summary: Abstract Motivation Accurate prediction of RNA 3D structures remains a central challenge in structural bioinformatics, necessitating reliable measures to quantify similarity between predicted models and experimentally determined reference structures. Currently, many scoring functions are available to assess different aspects of the tertiary structures of biomolecules. On the one hand, global measures average local irregularities, so that structures with distortions in different regions might generally be considered structurally similar. On the other hand, local conformational measures focus on specific inter-residue interactions and often fail to capture the broader topological context. Thus, there is a lack of methods capable of comprehensively assessing structural discrepancies across various spatial scales. Results To address this gap, we introduce Geometric Spherical Precision (GSP), a novel multi-scale score that assesses the quality of 3D RNA and RNP complex predictions. It integrates multiple partial scores computed from local geometric agreements into a single, easy-to-read, normalized score for ranking these predictions. We demonstrate that GSP reliably identifies models with comparable overall deviations, while maintaining strong agreement with global measures. These properties make it a useful tool for benchmarking and comparing 3D RNA structures and RNP complexes. Availability and Implementation The GSP script and evaluation results against state-of-the-art measures on the RNA-Puzzles and CASP15 datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19608328

all_papers.primary_summary_raw:
MOTIVATION: Accurate prediction of RNA 3D structures remains a central challenge in structural bioinformatics, necessitating reliable measures to quantify similarity between predicted models and experimentally determined reference structures. Currently, many scoring functions are available to assess different aspects of the tertiary structures of biomolecules. On the one hand, global measures average local irregularities, so that structures with distortions in different regions might generally be considered structurally similar. On the other hand, local conformational measures focus on specific inter-residue interactions and often fail to capture the broader topological context. Thus, there is a lack of methods capable of comprehensively assessing structural discrepancies across various spatial scales.

RESULTS: To address this gap, we introduce Geometric Spherical Precision (GSP), a novel multi-scale score that assesses the quality of 3D RNA and RNP complex predictions. It integrates multiple partial scores computed from local geometric agreements into a single, easy-to-read, normalized score for ranking these predictions. We demonstrate that GSP reliably identifies models with comparable overall deviations, while maintaining strong agreement with global measures. These properties make it a useful tool for benchmarking and comparing 3D RNA structures and RNP complexes.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The GSP script and evaluation results against state-of-the-art measures on the RNA-Puzzles and CASP15 datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19608328.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

all_papers.title: BioBatchNet: A Dual-Encoder Framework for Robust Batch Effect Correction in Imaging Mass Cytometry
all_papers.summary: Abstract Motivation Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC) is a cutting-edge technology for analysing spatially resolved protein expression at the single-cell level. However, its downstream analyses are often hindered by batch effects, which introduce systematic biases and obscure biological variations. Existing correction methods, largely developed for scRNA-seq data, face challenges in adapting to IMC data due to differences in data characteristics. Moreover, these methods struggle to achieve precise control, leading to either over-correction by removing critical biological information, or under-correction by leaving residual batch effects. Furthermore, IMC data often feature overlapping cell populations, complicating clustering and downstream analysis. These challenges underscore the need for a robust and controllable batch effect correction approach tailored to IMC data. Results We present BioBatchNet, a dual-encoder framework utilising adversarial training to explicitly disentangle batch-specific and biological signals. BioBatchNet enables controllable batch effect correction, balancing correction with preservation of biological variation. We evaluated BioBatchNet on three IMC datasets, where it outperformed seven benchmarking methods with robustness in both correction and biological signal conservation. Additionally, we developed a Constrained-Pairwise-Clustering (CPC) method, which employs constrained pairs to improve clustering performance, even in datasets with overlapping cell populations. To validate its generalisability, we adapted BioBatchNet for scRNA-seq datasets by altering the data likelihood from Gaussian to Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial distribution. This adapted version achieved competitive performance across four scRNA-seq datasets, obtaining the highest overall score on three of them. These results demonstrate BioBatchNet’s generalisability and robustness in correcting batch effects across diverse single-cell datasets and underscore its potential for large-scale biological analyses. Availability and Implementation The source code is available at https://github.com/UoM-HealthAI/BioBatchNet , with an archived snapshot on Zenodo (DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18783840 )

all_papers.primary_summary_raw: Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC) is a cutting-edge technology for analysing spatially resolved protein expression at the single-cell level. However, its downstream analyses are often hindered by batch effects, which introduce systematic biases and obscure biological variations. Existing correction methods, largely developed for scRNA-seq data, face challenges in adapting to IMC data due to differences in data characteristics. Moreover, these methods struggle to achieve precise control, leading to either over-correction by removing critical biological information, or under-correction by leaving residual batch effects. Furthermore, IMC data often feature overlapping cell populations, complicating clustering and downstream analysis. These challenges underscore the need for a robust and controllable batch effect correction approach tailored to IMC data. Results We present BioBatchNet, a dual-encoder framework utilising adversarial training to explicitly disentangle batch-specific and biological signals. BioBatchNet enables controllable batch effect correction, balancing correction with preservation of biological variation. We evaluated BioBatchNet on three IMC datasets, where it outperformed seven benchmarking methods with robustness in both correction and biological signal conservation. Additionally, we developed a Constrained-Pairwise-Clustering (CPC) method, which employs constrained pairs to improve clustering performance, even in datasets with overlapping cell populations. To validate its generalisability, we adapted BioBatchNet for scRNA-seq datasets by altering the data likelihood from Gaussian to Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial distribution. This adapted version achieved competitive performance across four scRNA-seq datasets, obtaining the highest overall score on three of them. These results demonstrate BioBatchNet’s generalisability and robustness in correcting batch effects across diverse single-cell datasets and underscore its potential for large-scale biological analyses.
